3.speaker: Deivid Wisci
3.text: "A very good morning to you, Mr. President. I trust I'm not imposing by arriving ahead of schedule?"

4.speaker: Narrator
4.text: As the morning sun streamed through the window of the Presidential Office, an imminent meeting loomed on my agenda. In a quarter of an hour, I was set to discuss the Energy Protection Act of 1932 with Ministers Graf, Holl, and Wisci.

14.speaker: Player
14.text: "Given the serious topic we're addressing, an early start might be just what we need."

16.speaker: Narrator
16.text: I was sipping my morning coffee and enjoying a quiet moment of solitude when Deivid arrived, characteristically early.

17.speaker: Player
17.text: "Not at all, Deivid. On the contrary, we've now got an extra few minutes to strategize before the meeting."

18.speaker: Narrator
18.text: The recent abrogation in the Grand National Assembly, coupled with ongoing dialogues with Gasom, had only served to amplify the discourse surrounding the legislation.

19.speaker: Deivid Wisci
19.text: "I appreciate your understanding, Mr. President. It's high time we addressed these pressing matters regarding the EPA."

22.speaker: Deivid Wisci
22.text: "I depart earlier for my appointments nowadays, as the stairs of the capital have become more of a challenge than I would like to admit."

23.speaker: Player
23.text: "Your wisdom rings true. It's been quite a rollercoaster since the election, hasn't it?"

24.speaker: Player
24.text: "Rest assured, Mr. Wisci. I intend to navigate these challenges with more finesse than my predecessors."

25.speaker: Player
25.text: “The Maroon District and the ministerial buildings are dispersed in a very artificial way. No wonder it takes longer.”

26.speaker: Player
26.text: “It's nothing to be ashamed of, Deivid. Would you like some coffee or tea?”

27.speaker: Player
27.text: "Well, Deivid, it's not the stairs we're battling, but the relentless march of time."

28.speaker: Deivid Wisci
28.text: "I've already had my tea today, as per my doctor's advice. She suggests chamomile in the morning and sage tea in the evening for optimal health."

29.speaker: Deivid Wisci
29.text: "Reflecting on the years I've spent within these walls is a journey in itself. From the time my father first brought me here during the reign of the King, right up to the present."

30.speaker: Deivid Wisci
30.text: "It wasn't always like this, you know. Before Tarquin Soll and his architect Herman Equa gave this area a neo-classical facelift and a new name, it used to be known as the Republic District. "

31.speaker: Deivid Wisci
31.text: “I will support you to the end of your term and beyond if my health allows.”
31.conditionsRaw: (Variable["BaseGame.Decision_Turn02_StatusReaction_WarnTraitors"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Reform_Autocrat_Path"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Decision_Turn02_StatusReaction_BoostPolice"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Turn02_FPnT_Consulate_Condemn"] == true) == false

32.speaker: Deivid Wisci
32.text: "I trust you're faring well. Sordland is akin to a wild mustang — complex, spirited, and ever elusive to rein in."

33.speaker: Player
33.text: "Or perhaps a stubborn mountain goat, unbudging and headstrong."

34.speaker: Deivid Wisci
34.text: "A public servant is bound by one principle alone. To serve, to be the voice and hand of the people."

35.speaker: Deivid Wisci
35.text: "Listening to the doctor does bring me some comfort. It feels as though my throat has been refreshed thanks to her."

36.speaker: Narrator
36.text: A colossal zeppelin traversed the sky above the Maroon District. For a fleeting moment, it blotted out the sun before gently veering to the left, letting light flood the office once more.

38.speaker: Symon Holl
38.conditionsRaw: Variable["BaseGame.Decision_Turn02_StatusReaction_WarnTraitors"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Reform_Autocrat_Path"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Decision_Turn02_StatusReaction_BoostPolice"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Turn02_FPnT_Consulate_Condemn"] == true

39.speaker: Symon Holl
39.conditionsRaw: (Variable["BaseGame.Decision_Turn02_StatusReaction_WarnTraitors"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Reform_Autocrat_Path"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Decision_Turn02_StatusReaction_BoostPolice"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Turn02_FPnT_Consulate_Condemn"] == true) == false

40.speaker: Deivid Wisci
40.text: “I will do my best to support you to the end of your term. This country deserves a fresh start and not a descent into the darkness of the distant past.”
40.conditionsRaw: Variable["BaseGame.Decision_Turn02_StatusReaction_WarnTraitors"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Reform_Autocrat_Path"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Decision_Turn02_StatusReaction_BoostPolice"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGame.Turn02_FPnT_Consulate_Condemn"] == true

41.speaker: Deivid Wisci
41.text: "I often ponder what will endure of our actions and identities. Do they hold any significance in the grand scheme of things?"

42.speaker: Narrator
42.text: His gaze drifted, locking onto something beyond the window.

43.speaker: Deivid Wisci
43.text: "I recall those days with such clarity. The city was a vision of beauty, its people radiant with hope. But the civil war shattered our Sordish Dream, exposing the darkest parts of our nature."

44.speaker: Deivid Wisci
44.text: “My grandmother was a farmer. Through her, I know that sturdy stubbornness and why the mystical Sordish Mountain Goat is our people's soul animal.”

45.speaker: Player
45.text: “I need loyal people to make the change this country deserves.”

46.speaker: Player
46.text: “The longest roads are travelled easier with the dearest fellows.”

47.speaker: Player
47.text: “Your expertise is very welcome in this administration. People abroad keep praising you.”

48.speaker: Narrator
48.text: He punctuated his statement with a cough, then reached for a glass of water and took a sip.

49.speaker: Deivid Wisci
49.text: "You crossed paths with Herman Equa at Holsord State University, didn't you? He was a mentor to many. I recall our discussions about the future at the Kabaret Lachaven, with him and Heron Garaci."

56.speaker: Deivid Wisci
56.text: “I know you were just a student at the Lachaven Business School, far from Holsord. But the armed rebels did reach your area.”

57.speaker: Deivid Wisci
57.text: “I know you were just a student at the Deyr University of Culture. Witnessing what true oppression was like.”

58.speaker: Deivid Wisci
58.text: "I did not agree with all of the measures enacted by the technocratic government of that era. But some were undeniably effective."

59.speaker: Deivid Wisci
59.text: "In the end, it took a collective effort to reassemble our nation's fragmented pieces. I'm sure you remember those dark days yourself."

60.speaker: Deivid Wisci
60.text: "A mountain goat, you say? Interesting analogy. They are indeed resilient, much like our nation."

61.speaker: Narrator
61.text: Just as the conversation hit a pause, the door swung open and the other ministers arrived. Symon Holl entered first with a confident stride.

62.speaker: Symon Holl
62.text: "Good morning, Mr. President. Deivid. I trust the discussion is progressing well?"

63.speaker: Narrator
63.text: Lileas followed closely behind. She walked in with an air of calm authority, her gaze sweeping across the room.

64.speaker: Lileas Graf
64.text: "Gentlemen. I hope I'm not interrupting anything crucial."

65.speaker: Player
65.text: "Still, one must credit Tarquin Soll for extricating our nation from the ashes."

66.speaker: Player
66.text: "Perhaps history would have taken a different course if the Izzam Incident hadn't happened."

67.speaker: Player
67.text: "We are deeply indebted to him. The principles of Sollism hold a special place in my heart and continue to guide my decisions."

72.speaker: Player
72.text: "Those were formative years for me. Equa and Garaci left an indelible mark on my outlook."

73.speaker: Player
73.text: "It's interesting how those academic days shape our perspectives, isn't it?"

74.speaker: Player
74.text: "It was a surreal time, studying business principles while chaos ensued just a few miles away."

75.speaker: Player
75.text: "Those disturbances did not deter me from my studies. In fact, they reinforced the importance of my education."

76.speaker: Player
76.text: "It was a difficult period. But it was also a reminder of the change I wished to see in Sordland."

77.speaker: Player
77.text: "Those experiences have shaped me, and they continue to inform my decisions as president."

78.speaker: Player
78.text: "In retrospect, an earlier resignation might have been beneficial. His ingrained traditions seem to have done more harm than good in the long run."

79.speaker: Deivid Wisci
79.text: "Indeed, the Izzam Incident is a reminder of how unforeseen events can rapidly change the course of a nation."

80.speaker: Deivid Wisci
80.text: "No one can deny Soll's contribution. His leadership was instrumental in rebuilding Sordland."

81.speaker: Deivid Wisci
81.text: "There's merit to that argument. The lingering influence of Soll's traditions may have hampered Alphonso's ability to bring about the changes he envisioned."

82.speaker: Deivid Wisci
82.text: "Sollism indeed has its virtues, and it's clear that Soll's legacy continues to resonate with many. The challenge for us is to learn from the past while forging our own path forward."

83.speaker: Deivid Wisci
83.text: "It turned us away from the path of reform, but we still worked hard to create the Sordland my father had envisioned."

84.speaker: Deivid Wisci
84.text: "Ah. I still remember the first airships in Sordland. We purchased them from Qinal after the war, during the birth of what Soll called the 'Second Republic'."

85.speaker: Deivid Wisci
85.text: "Our infrastructure lay in ruins, and those zeppelins offered a much-needed lifeline, a chance to traverse and rebuild. And then, thanks to our research council's diligent efforts, we started manufacturing our own in Gelsord."

86.speaker: Player
86.text: "It's fascinating to think how much we depended on foreign help after the war. We've come a long way since then."

87.speaker: Player
87.text: "The manufacturing of zeppelins in Gelsord was truly a turning point."

88.speaker: Player
88.text: "Do you think we might have leaned too heavily on zeppelins for our transportation needs? Perhaps we should have invested more in rebuilding our roads and railways."

89.speaker: Deivid Wisci
89.text: "We were in a desperate state then. But remember, it is often in our darkest hours that we find the strength to rise again."

90.speaker: Deivid Wisci
90.text: "You're quite right. It symbolized our resilience, our determination to regain our footing. It was a beacon of hope, signaling the revival of our battered industry."

91.speaker: Deivid Wisci
91.text: "An interesting point. Perhaps a more balanced approach would have served us better. In the aftermath of the civil war, it was often about immediate solutions, and the zeppelins offered just that."

95.speaker: Deivid Wisci
95.text: "At the time, the destroyed roads, bridges and all made air travel the most suitable option. But now I am glad that your presidency is focusing on building up our infrastructure."

96.speaker: Deivid Wisci
96.text: "But over time, he drifted away from the ideals of reform and progress that my father held so dear."

97.speaker: Deivid Wisci
97.text: "Our reliance on others was temporary, a stepping stone towards the self-sufficiency we achieved with the National Autarky Plan. Even though it had downsides, I still consider it a success."

98.speaker: Narrator
98.text: A pause fell over the room. Deivid's gaze landed on the portrait of Tarquin Soll hanging in the Presidential Office.

99.speaker: Player
99.text: "Those same amendments also opened the door to corruption."

100.speaker: Player
100.text: "Do you think the EPA still holds relevance today, or should we consider a complete overhaul?"

101.speaker: Player
101.text: "The NAP was a cornerstone for our post-war recovery. I wonder, could we have done more with it?"

102.speaker: Deivid Wisci
102.text: "Hindsight, as they say. We did what we believed was best at the time. Could we have done more? Perhaps."

103.speaker: Deivid Wisci
103.text: "Indeed, no policy is immune to misuse. Alphonso's amendments were ambitious, but they also left room for exploitation. We must remain vigilant against such risks."

104.speaker: Deivid Wisci
104.text: "The EPA has its roots in a different era. While some of its principles may still hold, we must not shy away from revising it in light of our current needs and challenges."

105.speaker: Narrator
105.text: His eyes lingered on the stern face of the old leader. A sigh escaped his lips.

106.speaker: Deivid Wisci
106.text: "Now, when I think of the EPA, my mind is carried back to the formative years of post-civil war Holsord in the 1930s. The debates, the passion, the potential for transformation—it was a time of renewed optimism."

107.speaker: Deivid Wisci
107.text: "It is our duty now to learn from the past and strive for a better future. What applied back then won't apply to now."

108.speaker: Deivid Wisci
108.text: "His visionary zeal succumbed to the more pragmatic, more conservative, and sometimes even regressive, dictates of political survival."

109.speaker: Player
109.text: "Life in Holsord back then was tough. Electricity blackouts, ruined infrastructure, unemployment, gangs..."

110.speaker: Player
110.text: "I remember that Soll's pardons to armed rebels did a lot to quell the rampant unrest."

111.speaker: Player
111.text: "I can see why the Energy Protection Act was so crucial at the time. We had to safeguard our energy sector from foreign interference, especially in the context of the post-civil-war economic situation."

112.speaker: Deivid Wisci
112.text: "It was a challenging period, yes, but we persevered together as a nation."

113.speaker: Deivid Wisci
113.text: "Soll's pardons were undoubtedly a contentious move, as they sparked debates about the extent of amnesty granted and the implications for justice."

114.speaker: Deivid Wisci
114.text: "Yes, the EPA helped ensure that the sector remained under our control, limiting the extent of ownership of foreign powers such as Rumburg or Lespia."

115.speaker: Deivid Wisci
115.text: "In a way, Tarquin Soll did carry on my father's legacy. Under his leadership, we transitioned from a military government to a civilian one, and experienced our first multi-party elections."

116.speaker: Deivid Wisci
116.text: “I am sure at least some of my wrinkles today were a direct result of my non-stop debates with them.”

117.speaker: Deivid Wisci
117.text: “Stability and order is important to our nation. Yet sometimes disorder is necessary for change."

118.speaker: Deivid Wisci
118.text: “The minorities of this nation have suffered particularly.”

119.speaker: Deivid Wisci
119.text: "My father was a visionary, a man who sought to modernize Sordland into a secular, democratic republic. I've always been guided by his principles."

120.speaker: Player
120.text: "Your father's legacy still looms large. Has it influenced your own views?"

121.speaker: Narrator
121.text: Deivid turned towards the large, framed portrait of his father, Artor Sanaco Wisci, hanging on the wall. Painted with rich, warm hues, it captured the first President of Sordland in his prime.

122.speaker: Narrator
122.text: A spark of determination gleamed in his eyes, and his mouth was set in a gentle, firm smile – a reflection of his belief in a better future for our country.

123.speaker: Deivid Wisci
123.text: "His ability to mobilize public support for revolutionary change has been a constant inspiration to me."

124.speaker: Player
124.text: "Sordland wouldn't be what it is today without your father."

125.speaker: Deivid Wisci
125.text: "Yes, my father's leadership laid the foundation for the Sordland we know. His policies were aimed at building a secular and democratic state where every citizen's rights are protected."

126.speaker: Deivid Wisci
126.text: "He believed in a Sordland that was modern and forward-looking. Everything he did was aimed at fostering progress, even his controversial embrace of foreign ideologies."

127.speaker: Player
127.text: "Artor S. Wisci. It's a shame that such an influential man died under such tragic circumstances."

128.speaker: Deivid Wisci
128.text: "Losing my father in the Holsord Prison fire was a turning point in my life. I was shocked when he was arrested, and his sudden death left a deep void."

129.speaker: Deivid Wisci
129.text: "But it also ignited a fire in me, a resolve to carry on his legacy and fight for the principles he stood for. The circumstances of his death are a stark reminder of the lengths to which those in power can go to silence dissent."

130.speaker: Narrator
130.text: He looked back at the portrait with a mix of pride and sadness.

131.speaker: Deivid Wisci
131.text: "It has made me wary, but also more committed to ensuring that such a tragedy does not repeat itself in our country."

132.speaker: Deivid Wisci
132.text: "Alphonso, for all his flaws, did seek to set the nation back on a path of progress with his focus on a free market and economic liberalization."

133.speaker: Deivid Wisci
133.text: "His EPA amendments, for example, were a severe departure from Soll's National Autarky Plan. But many praised the way that it opened the doors for unprecedented foreign investment in our energy economy."

134.speaker: Deivid Wisci
134.text: "Welcome, everyone. It's great to see you all here. We have some important discussions on the agenda today, particularly concerning the Energy Protection Act."

135.speaker: Player
135.text: "Thank you, Deivid. I appreciate the urgency. Let's get right to the heart of the matter."

136.speaker: Player
136.text: "Indeed, it's a critical issue that we need to address. I look forward to hearing everyone's perspectives."

138.speaker: Lileas Graf
138.text: "The Assembly has spoken on this matter, and as it stands, the Energy Protection Act of 1932 will not be repealed. It's clear that our colleagues have recognized the potential risks of exposing our energy sector to foreign ownership."

139.speaker: Lileas Graf
139.text: "While this doesn't end the debate, it does underline the importance of respecting our Assembly's decision."

140.speaker: Symon Holl
140.text: "Today, we have the opportunity to shape the economic strategy of Sordland for decades to come. The EPA has long stood as a key contention and debate point of the National Autarky Plan."

141.speaker: Symon Holl
141.text: "This matter is a discussion of how Sordland sees itself and how we position ourselves in the world. Our nation has taken very different economic approaches in the last four decades."

145.speaker: Symon Holl
145.text: "The President's decision to foster a planned economy provides us with significant insight into our policy direction."

146.speaker: Symon Holl
146.text: "Mr. President has decided to lean on promoting a market economy, which should give us a clear indicator."

147.speaker: Deivid Wisci
147.text: "I respect the decision of the Assembly, Lileas. However, we mustn't allow this setback to deter us from exploring our options. The global landscape is ever-evolving and we must adapt accordingly."

148.speaker: Symon Holl
148.text: "It's also important to remember that the Assembly's decision is not the final word. There is room for further legislative efforts and executive initiatives."

149.speaker: Player
149.text: "A fair point, Lileas. We must respect the decision of the Assembly, even if it doesn't align with our own views."

150.speaker: Player
150.text: "The Assembly's decision has been made, but that doesn't mean we will stop advocating for what we believe is right for Sordland."

151.speaker: Player
151.text: "It's disappointing to see the Assembly resist change this much. Our debate is definitely not over."

152.speaker: Symon Holl
152.text: "When it comes to the Energy Protection Act, I believe we should increase our threshold for foreign investment. In fact, my preference would be to remove the threshold entirely."

153.speaker: Symon Holl
153.text: "This would undoubtedly strengthen energy institutions such as Gasom and Sordish Petroleum. We've seen Rizia's interest in the former, and I know Lespia has had its eye on the latter for some time..."

154.speaker: Lileas Graf
154.text: "That's precisely what I'm worried about. We have to remember that we're dealing with national security as well as economics. Reverting to the Soll-era 10 percent limit or keeping the law as it is would be a safer approach."

155.speaker: Lileas Graf
155.text: "We cannot risk our energy infrastructure falling into foreign hands. Especially not to Rumburg!"

156.speaker: Deivid Wisci
156.text: "I see merit in both your arguments. Yes, we need to protect our national security, but we also need to consider the economic implications. Perhaps a mixed approach would work best?"

157.speaker: Deivid Wisci
157.text: "What if we increased the limit to 49 percent, thereby attracting foreign investment while maintaining Sordish control over critical energy sectors?"

158.speaker: Player
158.text: "Considering potential foreign buyers such as Qinal, Rizia, Anraka, Rumburg, and Lespia, what are the worst-case scenarios if they gain control over our hydroelectric, gas, and oil sectors?"

159.speaker: Player
159.text: "How would the Energy Protection Act changes impact corporations like Gasom, which could sell to any entity under the revised laws?"

160.speaker: Player
160.text: "Lileas, you mentioned national security risks. Could you elaborate further on that?"

161.speaker: Player
161.text: "How would changes to the Energy Protection Act affect energy prices within Sordland?"

162.speaker: Symon Holl
162.text: "The scenarios Lileas mentioned are possible, of course, but think about the economic growth and international relations that could be fostered."

163.speaker: Lileas Graf
163.text: "I believe you already know the answer to this, Mr. President."

164.speaker: Deivid Wisci
164.text: "There's no denying the potential risks of foreign buyers gaining control over critical sectors."

165.speaker: Deivid Wisci
165.text: "National security risks are always a concern when discussing foreign ownership. That's why it's crucial to have thorough vetting and monitoring processes in place."

166.speaker: Deivid Wisci
166.text: "With increased foreign investment, we could potentially see a decrease in energy prices."

167.speaker: Lileas Graf
167.text: "The national security risks are significant. Foreign entities could use their stake in our energy sector as leverage in diplomatic or economic negotiations."

168.speaker: Symon Holl
168.text: "Yes, Gasom could potentially sell to anyone, but wouldn't that be a show of the strength and attractiveness of our energy sector on the global stage?"

169.speaker: Lileas Graf
169.text: "Changing the Energy Protection Act could lead to increased energy prices, as foreign entities could manipulate the market."

170.speaker: Symon Holl
170.text: "With increased competition and foreign investment, we could also see a decrease in energy prices. The more players in the market, the more competitive the prices will be."

171.speaker: Lileas Graf
171.text: "I firmly believe in the sovereignty and strength of our nation."

172.speaker: Deivid Wisci
172.text: "Given the turbulent economic landscape, maintaining the status quo of the Energy Protection Act could offer us stability."

173.speaker: Symon Holl
173.text: "While I maintain that increasing foreign investment could significantly stimulate our economy."

183.speaker: Symon Holl
183.conditionsRaw: Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_ForeignTakeOver_Option1"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_GASOMImpact_Option2"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_NationalSecurityRisks_Option3"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_EnergyPrices_Option4"] == true

184.speaker: Symon Holl
184.conditionsRaw: (Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_ForeignTakeOver_Option1"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_GASOMImpact_Option2"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_NationalSecurityRisks_Option3"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_EnergyPrices_Option4"] == true) == false

185.speaker: Player
185.text: "We can proceed. It's time to settle this subject."
185.conditionsRaw: Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_ForeignTakeOver_Option1"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_GASOMImpact_Option2"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_NationalSecurityRisks_Option3"] == true  or  Variable["BaseGameIsolated.EPA_Hub_EnergyPrices_Option4"] == true

195.speaker: Player
195.text: "Let's remove the Energy Protection Act entirely. We need to drastically open up our energy economy to the world." [EPA REMOVED]

197.speaker: Symon Holl
197.text: "Should we decide to increase the EPA threshold to 49 percent or eliminate it entirely, it could spark an influx of foreign investment."

201.speaker: Symon Holl
201.text: "Even if we manage to stabilize our economy, loosening the EPA regulations could still be beneficial."

202.speaker: Lileas Graf
202.text: "A planned economy does not necessarily mean restricting foreign investment. It's about judicious management and control, ensuring that our nation's interests are always at the forefront."

203.speaker: Symon Holl
203.text: "We must remember that Sordland was facing an economic crisis during his tenure, and these changes provided a lifeline for our energy industries."

204.speaker: Player
204.text: "Wasn't this change a sign of desperation rather than a strategic move?"

205.speaker: Player
205.text: "But did the increased foreign ownership actually lead to substantial economic growth?"

206.speaker: Player
206.text: "I must confess, when the changes to the Energy Protection Act were first implemented, I harbored serious reservations."

207.speaker: Deivid Wisci
207.text: "It was a strategic decision aimed at modernizing our economy and promoting growth, while still preserving the core objective of the Act --protecting Sordland's energy sector."

208.speaker: Deivid Wisci
208.text: "It facilitated foreign investment and provided our industries with much-needed capital. The effects of such policy changes often take time to fully manifest, but they lay the groundwork for future economic development."

209.speaker: Deivid Wisci
209.text: "However, it's crucial to remember that policy-making often involves balancing competing interests and making tough decisions. The goal was, and remains, to advance Sordland's economy while protecting our strategic interests."

210.speaker: Deivid Wisci
210.text: "The economic crisis during Alphonso's tenure did necessitate action, but we should not view the change to the Energy Protection Act as simply a desperate measure."

211.speaker: Deivid Wisci
211.text: "While the increase in foreign ownership alone didn't lead to a drastic upturn in economic growth, it did have a positive effect."

212.speaker: Deivid Wisci
212.text: "Your reservations were not unfounded. It was indeed a significant change and, as with any policy shift, it brought about its share of controversies and criticisms."

213.speaker: Symon Holl
213.text: "Given our current economic predicament, this would be a significant boost."

214.speaker: Player
214.text: "I've always admired your devotion to Sordland, Lileas. It's clear that you have our nation's interests at heart."

215.speaker: Player
215.text: "While I respect your stance, Lileas, I must disagree. Despite my current support for it, I believe a planned economy could also hurt Sordland in the long run."

216.speaker: Player
216.text: "You present a compelling argument, Lileas. It's certainly an aspect we must consider moving forward."

217.speaker: Lileas Graf
217.text: "I appreciate your kind words, Mr. President. It's our shared dedication to Sordland that drives us."

218.speaker: Lileas Graf
218.text: "I think you are misguided in this way of thinking. But of course we're allowed to hold differing opinions."

219.speaker: Lileas Graf
219.text: "Thank you, Mr. President. It's crucial to consider all angles in matters as important as this."

223.speaker: Symon Holl
223.text: "By creating an attractive environment for foreign investors, we can ensure that Sordland is not merely surviving, but thriving in the long term."

224.speaker: Lileas Graf
224.text: "Promoting a market economy does not inherently translate to prosperity for all. It can lead to a concentration of wealth, with the rich getting richer while the middle and working classes struggle."

225.speaker: Lileas Graf
225.text: "We need to ensure that the benefits of economic growth are shared equitably across all layers of Sordish society."

226.speaker: Player
226.text: "I couldn't agree more, Lileas. The welfare of our citizens should be our primary concern."

227.speaker: Player
227.text: "I believe a free market fosters competition, which ultimately leads to innovation and economic growth."

228.speaker: Player
228.text: "Your perspective provides valuable insight. It's important that we consider all potential outcomes."

229.speaker: Lileas Graf
229.text: "I'm glad we see eye to eye on this matter, Mr. President. Our welfare as a whole depends on that of the least fortunate among us."

230.speaker: Lileas Graf
230.text: "I understand your point of view, Mr. President. But we must also consider the potential pitfalls of unregulated capitalism."

231.speaker: Lileas Graf
231.text: "Thank you, Mr. President. It's indeed crucial to consider all possibilities when making decisions of this magnitude."

232.speaker: Symon Holl
232.text: "Our current version of the Energy Protection Act dates back to 1949. President Alphonso's amendment raised the cap on foreign investment in Sordish energy companies up to 20 percent."

233.speaker: Symon Holl
233.text: "An increase to 49 percent could be a balanced compromise, signaling to the world that Sordland is open for business while retaining majority control of our assets. But some potential partners -- particularly ATO countries -- might regard even that as insufficient."

234.speaker: Lileas Graf
234.text: "Returning the threshold to 10 percent, as it was during the Soll era, could protect us from undue foreign influence and ensure that our energy sector remains in Sordish hands."

235.speaker: Deivid Wisci
235.text: "We are already open to foreign investment at a 20 percent threshold. Changing this percentage may introduce unexpected challenges and could complicate our foreign relations."

236.speaker: Player
236.text: "We will increase the foreign ownership threshold to 49 percent. This will increase foreign investment." [EPA AT 49]

237.speaker: Player
237.text: "Let's keep the Energy Protection Act as it is. The status quo has worked so far." [EPA KEPT AT 20]

238.speaker: Player
238.text: "We are returning the foreign ownership limit to 10 percent, as it was in the Soll era." [EPA TO 10]

239.speaker: Symon Holl
239.text: "This has the potential to spur significant economic growth."

241.speaker: Lileas Graf
241.text: "I fear this compromises our national energy sovereignty."

243.speaker: Deivid Wisci
243.text: "A balanced approach will serve us well."

244.speaker: Lileas Graf
244.text: "It's a substantial increase. I fear we are opening ourselves up too much. "

245.speaker: Symon Holl
245.text: "It's a safe choice, though it might limit our economic growth."

246.speaker: Deivid Wisci
246.text: "Stability is key in these uncertain times."

247.speaker: Lileas Graf
247.text: "It may not be what Soll would have wanted, but it is a prudent decision."

248.speaker: Symon Holl
248.text: "It's a conservative approach and it will limit our potential for growth. I will work hard to reduce the impact on our energy industry."

249.speaker: Deivid Wisci
249.text: "This will send a strong message of self-reliance."

250.speaker: Lileas Graf
250.text: "This ensures our energy resources remain firmly under Sordish control."

255.speaker: Narrator
255.text: The door to the room opened. Livia Suno carried a tray laden with an assortment of beverages.

256.speaker: Narrator
256.text: She was a little clumsy as she maneuvered around the room, refilling cups and glasses with tea, coffee, and water.

257.speaker: Livia Suno
257.text: "Excuse me, gentlemen and madam. I didn't mean to interrupt. What would you like to drink, Mr. President?"

258.speaker: Player
258.text: "Thank you, Livia. A coffee for me, please."

259.speaker: Player
259.text: "Appreciate it, Livia. Tea would be perfect now."

261.speaker: Livia Suno
261.text: "Of course, Mr. President. Here you are."

262.speaker: Livia Suno
262.text: "Very well, Mr. President. Here's your tea."

264.speaker: Narrator
264.text: Livia finished serving the beverages and retreated towards the door. She glanced around the room one last time before quietly backing out.

265.speaker: Narrator
265.text: The meeting resumed, our conversation growing slightly louder over the clink of cups and glasses.

266.speaker: Player
266.text: "Please be more considerate and ask before you enter next time."

267.speaker: Livia Suno
267.text: "I'm sorry, I will. I thought the meeting had ended and wanted to refill the refreshments."

271.speaker: Symon Holl
271.text: "I share your sentiments, Mr. President. However, we must be careful to avoid encouraging anti-business tendencies."

272.speaker: Deivid Wisci
272.text: "While we are here, I will inform you all that I've been lending my expertise to Minister Beniwoll in relation to the Workers Rights Bill."

273.speaker: Lileas Graf
273.text: "I concur, Mr. President. Ensuring the rights of our workers is paramount, although we must be cautious of any hidden agendas."

274.speaker: Player
274.text: "Your collaboration with Mr. Beniwoll is commendable. I hope it will bring about a positive change for our workforce."

275.speaker: Player
275.text: "Workers' rights are important, but we need to ensure that the bill doesn't introduce excessive regulations that could stifle our businesses."

276.speaker: Player
276.text: "I will reserve my judgment until I have a chance to review the bill in detail."

277.speaker: Deivid Wisci
277.text: "Thank you, Mr. President. The bill aims to prioritize workers' wellbeing. It's a step towards a more humane economic system."

278.speaker: Deivid Wisci
278.text: "I understand your concerns, Mr. President. We are aiming to strike a balance between workers' rights and business needs."

279.speaker: Deivid Wisci
279.text: "Absolutely, Mr. President. We will ensure you receive the bill for review as soon as possible."

280.speaker: Symon Holl
280.text: "Agreed. The last thing we need is to overburden our businesses with regulations."

281.speaker: Symon Holl
281.text: "It's important not to decide these things too hastily. Don't let emotions cloud your judgement."

282.speaker: Lileas Graf
282.text: "Regulations are what prevent our businesses from exploiting vulnerable citizens, Mr. Holl."

283.speaker: Lileas Graf
283.text: "That's never a concern with you, is it, Mr. Holl?"

284.speaker: Symon Holl
284.text: "Anyway. I have been working on our upcoming term budget meeting and a proposal for business taxation changes."

285.speaker: Symon Holl
285.text: "Specifically, we're considering a range of 10 percent tax changes for small-to-medium enterprises and large corporations. This could be a significant move for our economic landscape."

286.speaker: Player
286.text: "Such a taxation approach could indeed invigorate our economy. But we must ensure it doesn't burden our SMEs unduly."

287.speaker: Player
287.text: "We should be careful with large changes to taxation. They could have unintended consequences."

288.speaker: Symon Holl
288.text: "I appreciate your insight, Mr. President. Ensuring the survival and growth of our SMEs is at the forefront of our considerations."

290.speaker: Deivid Wisci
290.text: "Tax changes could indeed have a significant impact on our economy. We must consider their implications carefully."

291.speaker: Deivid Wisci
291.text: "As a proponent of global trade and economic cooperation, I too believe we should be cautious about imposing excessive taxes on businesses."

292.speaker: Player
292.text: "I'm very satisfied that we are executing bold changes under this administration."

293.speaker: Symon Holl
293.text: "Bold changes can often lead to significant advancement. It shows that our government has vision and a willingness to embrace innovation."

294.speaker: Deivid Wisci
294.text: "We should explore alternative strategies that promote growth while ensuring corporations contribute their fair share."

295.speaker: Lileas Graf
295.text: "Large private corporations have enjoyed significant benefits and loopholes for far too long. They should pay their fair share."

296.speaker: Lileas Graf
296.text: "In light of the economic challenges we face, increasing taxation could provide much-needed revenue to support crucial public services and social welfare programs."

297.speaker: Lileas Graf
297.text: "To me, promoting growth comes secondary to holding corporations accountable."

298.speaker: Lileas Graf
298.text: "Meanwhile, Mr. President, I've heard about the plans for the Emergency Act. I believe it is a necessary step in ensuring the security and stability of Sordland."

299.speaker: Lileas Graf
299.text: "As such, I have already begun drafting the necessary action plans."

300.speaker: Player
300.text: "Excellent work, Lileas. We need to be prepared for all contingencies."

301.speaker: Player
301.text: "The Emergency Act is a serious measure. I trust you to handle it carefully."

302.speaker: Player
302.text: "Make sure to keep us all informed about your progress, Lileas."

303.speaker: Lileas Graf
303.text: "Thank you, Mr. President. I understand the gravity of the situation and am committed to ensuring the safety of our nation."

304.speaker: Lileas Graf
304.text: "I understand your concern, Mr. President. I assure you, I will handle this task with utmost care."

305.speaker: Lileas Graf
305.text: "Of course, Mr. President. You will be updated about every step we take."

306.speaker: Symon Holl
306.text: "I appreciate your diligence. Let's hope that the impact on our economy will be minimal."

307.speaker: Symon Holl
307.text: "The Emergency Act is a serious measure indeed. It's good to know you're handling it."

308.speaker: Symon Holl
308.text: "Keep the economic consequences in mind as you proceed, Lileas. We need to maintain a balance."

309.speaker: Deivid Wisci
309.text: "I trust you, Lileas. Just remember the potential impact on our international relations."

310.speaker: Deivid Wisci
310.text: "Handle it carefully, Lileas. We need to ensure the Emergency Act doesn't harm our diplomatic relations."

311.speaker: Deivid Wisci
311.text: "And please keep us informed. We all need to be in the loop."

312.speaker: Narrator
312.text: As the ministers rose from their seats, the late-morning light spilled into the room through the ornate windows.

313.speaker: Narrator
313.text: It seemed to signal the conclusion of the meeting.

314.speaker: Player
314.text: "Thank you all for your insights and collaboration today. Have a great afternoon."

315.speaker: Player
315.text: "Our unity is our strength. Let's continue to work together for the good of Sordland."

316.speaker: Player
316.text: "We've made some important decisions today. Let's wrap up for now and reconvene later if needed."

317.speaker: Player
317.text: "Our work is our legacy. Let's make sure it's one that Sordland can be proud of."

318.speaker: Lileas Graf
318.text: "Thank you for the discussion. I'll continue working on our priorities. Goodbye, everyone."

319.speaker: Symon Holl
319.text: "See you at the term budget meeting."

320.speaker: Deivid Wisci
320.text: "Until next time, dear colleagues. Take care and see you soon."

323.speaker: Deivid Wisci
323.text: "I believe it's crucial to ensure fair treatment for our workforce. And it is nearing presentation."

324.speaker: Player
324.text: "I heavily disagreed with the move at the time. Even as executive Vice President in 1946, Alphonso simply tried to change the country too fast."

325.speaker: Player
325.text: "First it was the State Educators Corps, then the SSC Bills, and then slowly the EPA. He wanted to erase every trace of Tarquin Soll's Second Republic."

327.speaker: Lileas Graf
327.text: "Gasom could fall under foreign control, just like any other energy corporation."

328.speaker: Deivid Wisci
328.text: "If we increase the foreign ownership threshold to 49%, we can attract more investments while mitigating those risks."

329.speaker: Deivid Wisci
329.text: "But we should also consider the potential impact on job security and national control of our energy sector."

330.speaker: Symon Holl
330.text: "While we may see entities from Qinal, Rizia, Anraka, Rumburg, or Lespia as potential threats, it's also crucial to see them as potential partners."

331.speaker: Symon Holl
331.text: "And those resources could be channeled into further development of our energy sector."

332.speaker: Lileas Graf
332.text: "I caution against drastic changes that may leave us vulnerable to foreign influence. We must maintain control of our energy sector at all costs."

333.speaker: Lileas Graf
333.text: "Our investment in Gasom reinforces Sordland's sovereignty. However, altering the EPA may dilute that sovereignty."

334.speaker: Deivid Wisci
334.text: "Considering we're investing heavily in Gasom, our decision about the EPA will greatly impact the attractiveness of the remaining shares to foreign investors."

335.speaker: Lileas Graf
335.text: "However, if we raise the foreign ownership threshold, we must be wary of the influence of Rumburg."

336.speaker: Lileas Graf
336.text: "Sharing the burden with Rizia does provide some reassurance."

337.speaker: Deivid Wisci
337.text: "With Sordland and Rizia co-investing in Gasom, there's a chance to build a partnership that benefits both our economies. However, how we adjust the EPA could significantly impact the outcome."

338.speaker: Lileas Graf
338.text: "If we raise the threshold, we risk inviting even more foreign control over our resources."

339.speaker: Lileas Graf
339.text: "Having Rizia as the sole investor already compromises our energy independence to a certain extent."

340.speaker: Deivid Wisci
340.text: "With Rizia being the sole investor, our position on the EPA will directly affect their stake. We must consider the potential outcomes and their implications on our energy independence."
340.conditionsRaw: ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_CoInvestmentRizia"] == true) == false) and (Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_OnlyRiziaInvestment"] == true) and ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_LargeSordlandInvestmentAlone"] == true) == false)

341.speaker: Player
341.text: "Considering Rizia's investment, we could stick with the current threshold. This way, we minimize foreign interference while keeping our energy sector financially stable."

342.speaker: Player
342.text: "Raising the threshold could attract more investors. However, we must be careful to avoid losing control of our resources."

343.speaker: Player
343.text: "Our partnership with Rizia has proven beneficial. I suggest we maintain the current threshold. Let's not make hasty decisions that might disrupt this balance."

344.speaker: Player
344.text: "Perhaps we should consider removing the threshold altogether. It could propel Gasom into the global market and truly maximize our gains."

345.speaker: Player
345.text: "If we keep the foreign ownership threshold as is, we're limiting foreign investment. However, our 30 percent stake in Gasom would remain significant and protected."

346.speaker: Player
346.text: "By reducing the foreign ownership limit to 10 percent, we're closing off most foreign investment opportunities. This ensures our 30 percent stake in Gasom holds significant power."

347.speaker: Deivid Wisci
347.text: "On the other hand, foreign investment would result in increased resources flowing to Gasom and its ilk."

348.speaker: Player
348.text: "By increasing the foreign ownership threshold to 49 percent, we're opening up more opportunities for foreign investment. This could improve the value of our own 30 percent stake in Gasom."

349.speaker: Player
349.text: "While your points are valid, Lileas, we can't ignore the potential economic benefits. Raising the threshold could attract more investors and increase the value of our shares."

350.speaker: Player
350.text: "Let's consider lowering the threshold back to 10 percent. This could ensure more Sordish control over Gasom and safeguard our energy independence."

351.speaker: Symon Holl
351.text: "I would say we've covered the implications of your EPA decision fairly thoroughly, Mr. President."
351.conditionsRaw: ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_CoInvestmentRizia"] == true) == false) and ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_OnlyRiziaInvestment"] == true) == false) and ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_LargeSordlandInvestmentAlone"] == true) == false)

352.speaker: Lileas Graf
352.text: "Raising the threshold to 49 percent could increase Gasom's value, and by extension the value of our 30 percent stake. But we don't want to lose control over the company."

353.speaker: Symon Holl
353.text: "A 49 percent threshold could increase the value of our stake without risking loss of control."

354.speaker: Deivid Wisci
354.text: "Increasing the EPA to 49% opens up a new avenue of trade, but we will have to ensure our national interests are not compromised."

355.speaker: Player
355.text: "We have to consider the long-term impact of our decisions. Foreign investment might bring immediate financial gains, but we'd risk losing control of our energy sector."

356.speaker: Lileas Graf
356.text: "Preserving the status quo ensures that our 30 percent stake remains significant, yes."

357.speaker: Symon Holl
357.text: "But would we be missing out on potential growth?"

358.speaker: Deivid Wisci
358.text: "You are both right. Keeping the status quo ensures stability, but we must weigh this against the potential trade opportunities we might be missing out on."

359.speaker: Lileas Graf
359.text: "Reducing the threshold to 10 percent would be my preference. It allows for the possibility for foreign investment while preserving Sordish sovereignty."

360.speaker: Symon Holl
360.text: "On the other hand, it would deter foreign investors, which would make a dent in the company's profitability and shrink our returns."

361.speaker: Deivid Wisci
361.text: "A 10 percent limit might offer protection, but we need to consider the potential economic isolation that could result."

362.speaker: Lileas Graf
362.text: "Maintaining the current threshold is a safe option, but my preference would be 10 percent default imposed in the Soll era. It will limit opportunities in the long run, but our state will perservere."

363.speaker: Symon Holl
363.text: "The current threshold provides a balance. It allows some level of foreign investment without risking too much foreign influence. Reverting to the past will lose us too many opportunities."

364.speaker: Deivid Wisci
364.text: "While maintaining the status quo provides stability, it might limit our potential for economic growth and trade relations."

365.speaker: Lileas Graf
365.text: "President, I must express my strong disagreement. Complete removal of the threshold means we would lose control over our own resources to foreign powers. It's too high a price for questionable economic benefits."

366.speaker: Symon Holl
366.text: "Removing the threshold is indeed an ambitious move, Mr. President. It could lead to a significant influx of foreign investment and boost our economy. However, we must be prepared to manage the associated risks and ensure our interests are not compromised."

367.speaker: Deivid Wisci
367.text: "A full removal, while certainly bold, could dramatically shift our international trade dynamics. It would also require us to navigate the complexities of increased foreign relations and potential dependency."

368.speaker: Lileas Graf
368.text: "I understand the potential economic benefits, but we can't compromise our sovereignty for profits."

369.speaker: Symon Holl
369.text: "Increasing the threshold might attract more foreign investors and increase the value of our stake. But of course we should ensure that Sordland's interests are safeguarded."

370.speaker: Deivid Wisci
370.text: "Opting for a more balanced approach aligns well with our objective of maintaining positive trade relations without compromising our sovereignty."

371.speaker: Player
371.text: "We should be more aggressive in attracting foreign investment. After all, a thriving energy sector can be a major driver of our economic growth."

372.speaker: Lileas Graf
372.text: "Maintaining the status quo might indeed be the safest choice in this scenario. We need to protect our energy sector from becoming a playground for foreign powers."

373.speaker: Symon Holl
373.text: "Keeping the current threshold could ensure a stable inflow of foreign investment without risking a major disruption in the energy sector."

374.speaker: Deivid Wisci
374.text: "Maintaining the status quo could provide stability in our relations with Rizia, but it might also limit our potential to attract additional foreign investment."

375.speaker: Symon Holl
375.text: "If we manage the risks effectively, raising the threshold could indeed provide a significant boost to our economy."

376.speaker: Deivid Wisci
376.text: "Raising the threshold could potentially boost our economy, but it could also complicate our relations with other foreign powers, including Rumburg."

377.speaker: Deivid Wisci
377.text: "Lowering the threshold could send a strong message of our commitment to national sovereignty, but it could also deter foreign investors."

378.speaker: Symon Holl
378.text: "Lowering the threshold might limit foreign investment, but it could also safeguard our energy sector from foreign exploitation."

379.speaker: Lileas Graf
379.text: "Attracting more investors at the cost of our energy independence is not a risk we should take. We cannot gamble with our nation's sovereignty."

380.speaker: Lileas Graf
380.text: "Returning to the 10 percent threshold would be a step in the right direction. It will ensure that Sordland remains in control of its own resources."

381.speaker: Player
381.text: "Our choices aren't just about the numbers. They hold significant implications for the people of Sordland. We must make our decision with them in mind."

382.speaker: Player
382.text: "The EPA has been a safeguard for our national interests, but we must also be open to change. We need to carefully weigh the benefits and drawbacks."

383.speaker: Deivid Wisci
383.text: "However, it's worth acknowledging that by offering clemency, Soll aimed to provide an opportunity for healing and reconciliation in a divided society."

384.speaker: Deivid Wisci
384.text: "Despite the controversies, it was crucial to our recovery and has helped us maintain our energy independence to this day."

385.speaker: Player
385.text: "The future of our gas industry lies in our hands, not anyone else's. Our full investment in Gasom demonstrates this."

386.speaker: Player
386.text: "By investing alone, we've seized significant control of the private gas sector. This aligns with our goal of nationalizing key industries. We must ensure this doesn't strain our economy."

387.speaker: Player
387.text: "This investment signifies our commitment to Sordland's energy independence. Let's put our resources to work for the Sordish people."

397.speaker: Player
397.text: "A joint venture with Rizia is a strategic move, not a concession. It's a partnership that secures our place in the global energy landscape."

398.speaker: Player
398.text: "Sharing investment responsibilities with Rizia may ease our financial load, but it also means we've invited foreign influence into our energy sector. We must tread carefully."

399.speaker: Player
399.text: "Our partnership with Rizia is our commitment to regional cooperation. It's a pragmatic move that will be beneficial for both nations."

400.speaker: Player
400.text: "There's wisdom in caution. Let's keep our options open and observe Rizia's approach. Our time to invest will come."

401.speaker: Player
401.text: "In these uncertain times, it's prudent to withhold our resources. Let's let Rizia navigate these turbulent waters first."

402.speaker: Player
402.text: "Our decision not to invest at this time is not a withdrawal but a strategic pause. We will decide when the time is right."

403.speaker: Narrator
403.conditionsRaw: ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_CoInvestmentRizia"] == true) == false) and ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_OnlyRiziaInvestment"] == true) == false) and ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_LargeSordlandInvestmentAlone"] == true) == false)

407.speaker: Symon Holl
407.text: "One more concern. Gus and Mikail informed me that you have given President Alphonso assurances about not imposing stricter EPA regulations."

408.speaker: Symon Holl
408.text: "Given the economic climate, it might be prudent not to destabilize the system. Imposing a reduction of the threshold would irreversibly harm Gasom."

409.speaker: Player
409.text: "There is no need to be destructive in an already dangerous economy that could spiral downward."

410.speaker: Player
410.text: "I understand the need for economic stability. But I'm reconsidering my promise now that I know all the facts."

411.speaker: Lileas Graf
411.text: "Our actions should be guided by the best interests of our nation."

412.speaker: Symon Holl
412.text: "We must consider the far-reaching implications of our actions. Especially in light of our recent dealings with Gasom."

413.speaker: Symon Holl
413.text: "Mr. President, your decision to position Sordland as the sole Gasom investor certainly gives us more control over the gas sector, but it has increased our financial burden significantly. We must review our fiscal policies."

414.speaker: Symon Holl
414.text: "Mr. President, your decision to pursue co-investment with Rizia allows us to distribute the financial burden and mitigate risks. It also promotes regional cooperation, aligning well with our fiscal policies."

415.speaker: Symon Holl
415.text: "Mr. President, your decision not to invest has certainly reduced our immediate financial responsibilities, but we may have missed an opportunity."
415.conditionsRaw: ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_CoInvestmentRizia"] == true) == false) and (Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_OnlyRiziaInvestment"] == true) and ((Variable["BaseGame.Turn03_EnT_Gasom_LargeSordlandInvestmentAlone"] == true) == false)

416.speaker: Player
416.text: "Our administration needs to protect the jobs of Gasom workers and this investment ensures that. I have little interest beyond this."

417.speaker: Player
417.text: "Rizia might not be the best partner given our history with them, but we have to take a balanced approach with our budget and economy."

418.speaker: Player
418.text: "By allowing Rizia to monopolize the energy sector, we've indirectly promoted capitalist exploitation. We must remain vigilant and ensure our people are not subjugated to foreign profiteering."

419.speaker: Deivid Wisci
419.text: "A reduction in the EPA could pave the way for potential profits from shares, whereas total removal may invite an unpredictable rush for the remaining 45%."

420.speaker: Player
420.text: "If we remove the Energy Protection Act entirely, our 30 percent investment could potentially be overshadowed by foreign investors. However, it could also maximize our returns if foreign investment floods in."

421.speaker: Lileas Graf
421.text: "Full removal of the EPA is a risk. Foreign investors could buy up larger stakes than our own. We might lose control over Gasom."

422.speaker: Symon Holl
422.text: "Eliminating the EPA could stimulate our economy, increasing the value of our 30 percent stake. But losing control over Gasom would be a heavy blow."

423.speaker: Deivid Wisci
423.text: "Foreign influence in Gasom, if not managed correctly, could lead to a dilution of Sordland's control in the energy sector."

424.speaker: Player
424.text: "Even though we're sharing the investment with Rizia, we should still prioritize Sordish control. Let's consider reducing the foreign ownership limit."

425.speaker: Lileas Graf
425.text: "I'm glad you see the risks, Mr. President. Keeping our energy sector in Sordish hands should be our priority."

426.speaker: Symon Holl
426.text: "Reducing the foreign ownership limit might safeguard our control, but it could limit our potential for economic growth."

427.speaker: Deivid Wisci
427.text: "Completely removing the EPA could upset our foreign relations, particularly with market economies. We must consider the implications of such an aggressive move."

428.speaker: Player
428.text: "We could remove the threshold entirely, opening up to more foreign investment. But we'd need to be prepared for all the diplomatic consequences that may follow."

429.speaker: Deivid Wisci
429.text: "It could also lead to a volatile situation in terms of our foreign relations."

430.speaker: Symon Holl
430.text: "Full removal of the threshold is an extremely bold move. It could lead to a significant increase in foreign investment, but we must also consider the risks."

431.speaker: Lileas Graf
431.text: "Total removal of the threshold is a dangerous proposition. It would make us vulnerable to foreign influence and could lead to the loss of our energy independence."

432.speaker: Player
432.text: "Our priority should be balancing the need for economic growth with maintaining national sovereignty. Perhaps a phased approach to increasing foreign ownership could be the answer."

433.speaker: Symon Holl
433.text: "Mr. President, it's time for us to make a decision. What will we do with the EPA?"

434.speaker: Player
434.text: "We need to balance our commitment to Alphonso with the needs of our nation."

435.speaker: Player
435.text: "There's also the matter of international perception. We should be careful not to appear as if we're making policy based on corporate interests alone."

448.speaker: Symon Holl
448.text: "I foresee difficult conversations ahead with the National Business Council and President Alphonso."

513.speaker: Player
513.text: "I'd like to clear my mind before the ministers arrive."

514.speaker: Deivid Wisci
514.text: "As you wish, Mr. President. I will be as silent as a mouse."

515.speaker: Narrator
515.text: Then the door swung open, ushering in the arrival of the other ministers. Symon Holl entered first with a confident stride.

516.speaker: Narrator
516.text: It was nice to sit in silence and enjoy each other's company. Time passed.

517.speaker: Deivid Wisci
517.text: "I believe much of his urgency was motivated by his own desire to escape Soll's shadow. For better or worse, he managed it."

518.speaker: Symon Holl
518.text: "Mr. President, Lileas, shall we return to the subject of the EPA?"

519.speaker: Symon Holl
519.text: "In my view, it was a necessary step to attract foreign investment and stimulate our economy."

520.speaker: Lileas Graf
520.text: "Think about it, Mr. President. If any one of those countries -- but especially Rumburg -- gains control of our energy sector, they could cut off our power at any moment."

521.speaker: Lileas Graf
521.text: "We would also be forced to comply with any decision they made regarding prices or environmental measures."

522.speaker: Symon Holl
522.text: "Don't forget about the importance of economic security. In a globalized world, economic strength can be just as critical as military might."

523.speaker: Symon Holl
523.text: "But yes, it's essential to maintain strict oversight and regulations to ensure national interests aren't compromised."

524.speaker: Deivid Wisci
524.text: "At times the window of change is only very small. And now that you and I are in the cabinet, we can promote the change we truly advocate for."

565.speaker: Player
565.text: "While I respect your stance, Lileas, I must disagree."

566.speaker: Lileas Graf
566.text: "I think you are misguided in this way of thinking. But of course we're allowed to hold differing opinions."

567.speaker: Player
567.text: "I share your view. Soll's old policy was choking the growth of Sordish energy businesses."

568.speaker: Deivid Wisci
568.text: "Many others also saw Alphonso's changes as necessary. Though they did not pass without a great deal of controversy."

569.speaker: Deivid Wisci
569.text: "In the end, the changes to the EPA did facilitate foreign investment, even if they didn't lead to a drastic uptick in economic growth."

570.speaker: Player
570.text: "I don't only respect the Assembly's decision. I wholeheartedly support it."

575.speaker: Symon Holl
575.text: "If we aim to deal more closely with Lespia, for example, I very much doubt they'll settle for a mere 49% energy investment."
